Theme

Money, work & business

go bankrupt verb

also bankrupt, bankruptcy, declare bankruptcy, insolvent, be broke

classical

Cic. Phil. 2.18: tenēsne memoriā praetextātum tē dēcoxisse? (Lewis & Short: “to become a bankrupt”)
Traupman 276

dēcoquō, dēcoquere, dēcoxī, dēcoctum

verb, third conjugation · Conjugation on Wiktionary

go bankrupt (literally “boil away”)

Other words

  • dēcoctor, dēcoctōris m. — a bankrupt, a ruined spendthrift

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Phil. 2.18; Cic. Cat. 2.3; Catull. 41.4 (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

  • bonam cōpiam ējūrāre — declare oneself insolvent (on oath)

    also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 9.16.7 (Lewis & Short s.v. cōpia: “to declare one’s self exempt through poverty”); Traupman 276

  • dēcoctiō, dēcoctiōnis f. — insolvency (late legal Latin); first a boiling down

    noun, third declension · also used · late Latin · Cod. Just. 11.9.5: ūnīus dēcoctiōnī ūniversī respondēre cōgentur; cf. Cod. Theod. 4.9.3 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 276 · Declension on Wiktionary

    Lewis & Short gives the word first of boiling down, in medical writers, and glosses the law codes’ use as “a decoction, mixture”; but there all are made answerable for one man’s dēcoctiō, which reads as his insolvency, the noun of dēcoquere, go bankrupt. Late, but with ancient warrant for Traupman’s sense.

SourcesLewis & Short: decoquo · Lewis & Short: decoctor · Lewis & Short: copia · Lewis & Short: decoctio

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency (printed page numbers): p. 276.

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
